title: Best Sealant for Cinder Block Walls (2026): 7 Sealers Ranked
h1: The 7 Best Cinder Block Sealers in 2026
keywords: best sealer for cinder block walls
best exterior cement block sealer and paint
description: The best sealant for cinder block walls is DRYLOK Extreme, maker-rated for 15 psi, for seeping basements, and Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 for exterior block.
dek: The best sealant for cinder block walls is DRYLOK Extreme, maker-rated for 15 psi, for seeping basements, and Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 for exterior block.
intro: The best cinder block sealer for exterior and above-grade walls is Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500, a silane-siloxane repellent that soaks into the block and leaves it looking untouched. For basement block that seeps after rain, DRYLOK Extreme is the better tool, because its maker rates it to resist 15 psi of water pressure from behind.

Those two picks show the first decision every block wall needs. Block is hollow, thirsty and laced with mortar joints, so you either soak it with an invisible repellent that stops rain getting in, or brush on a thick waterproof coating that holds back water pushing through. Where the wall is and which side the water comes from decides which one works.
quickAnswer: For exterior block, garage walls and retaining wall faces, buy Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 or the cheaper Foundation Armor SX5000. For interior basement block that seeps, brush on DRYLOK Extreme. Use Seal-Once Nano+Poly where odor matters, RadonSeal for mixed block and poured concrete, MasonryDefender for houses that mix block with brick or stone, and Ames Block and Wall where hairline cracks need a flexible coating.

blocks.p: Above grade, where rain hits the face of the wall, a penetrating repellent is the right cinder block sealer. Below grade on the inside of a basement, where water arrives from wet soil behind the block, you need a waterproof coating with a pressure rating.

Mixing those up is the most common reason a sealed block wall still gets wet. A repellent on the inside of a seeping basement wall does very little, and a thick coating on an exterior wall that only needed rain protection changes its look for no gain.

sections.h: The 7 Best Cinder Block Sealers in 2026, Ranked

blocks.p: Picks are ranked on what makers publish (active ingredients, coverage on block, pressure ratings, cure times), how well each chemistry suits porous block, and recurring owner feedback. Claims are attributed to the manufacturers; none of these were run through a lab here.

Siloxa-Tek 8500 is the product to beat on above-grade block. It is a penetrating silane-siloxane repellent, and that blend suits block well: siloxane handles the large surface pores of an open-textured unit while silane reaches deeper. Together they line the pores with a water-shedding treatment instead of laying a film on top. The wall looks the same but sheds rain, which cuts the soak-and-freeze cycle that cracks face shells and the wicking that leaves white efflorescence. Ghostshield markets it for block, concrete, brick and pavers, inside and out. Its limit is shared by every repellent: it is not a barrier against water pushed through the wall from saturated soil. It also tends to block paint adhesion, so decide on color before you seal. Owners commonly report strong beading on exterior block.
**Pros:** Blend suited to porous block and mortar; no film or visible change on most block; breathable; helps reduce efflorescence, spalling and freeze-thaw damage; also works on brick and pavers.
**Cons:** Not meant for water under pressure; can make later painting difficult; needs bare, clean, absorbent masonry.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Ghostshield+Siloxa-Tek+8500&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Basement Block: DRYLOK Extreme Masonry Waterproofer

blocks.p: On the inside of a basement block wall, water arrives from behind, so a repellent is the wrong tool. DRYLOK Extreme is made for this. It is a thick masonry waterproofer that the manufacturer rates to withstand 15 psi of hydrostatic pressure, more than most residential walls with working gutters ever see. Application decides the result: the label calls for scrubbing the first coat into the block with a stiff nylon brush until every pinhole is filled, then adding a second coat. On block, that scrubbing matters even more than on poured concrete, because the open texture is full of voids a roller skips. It dries to a paint-like finish you can leave as is or tint, so it covers moisture control and appearance in one product. It cannot stop water at the floor joint, and it fails early over efflorescence or old paint.
**Pros:** Maker-rated for 15 psi; fills pores and pinholes when brushed in; acts as barrier and finish coat; tintable and widely sold.
**Cons:** Changes the look of the wall; needs bare masonry free of paint and efflorescence; brushing block is slow, tiring work.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=DRYLOK+Extreme+Masonry+Waterproofer&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Value Repellent: Foundation Armor SX5000

blocks.p: SX5000 competes directly with the Ghostshield pick and often costs a little less. It works the same way: the silane-siloxane blend soaks into block, brick and concrete and leaves a water-repellent treatment inside the pores instead of a coating, so the wall looks unchanged and keeps breathing. Foundation Armor sells it with different carriers. The water-based version is easier to live with indoors and in tight spaces, while solvent-based sealers can get into dense surfaces more readily but need strong ventilation and no ignition sources nearby. It suits exterior block walls, garage walls and the exposed faces of retaining walls, where rain and splash are the main threats. Like any repellent, it will not hold back water from wet soil on a basement wall and may prevent painting later. Owners often mention easy pump-sprayer application.
**Pros:** Silane-siloxane blend for depth and surface protection; no visible film; helps against water, salt and freeze-thaw; water- and solvent-based versions.
**Cons:** Solvent version smells strongly indoors; no resistance to water pressure from the soil side; can block paint adhesion.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Foundation+Armor+SX5000&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Silicate Option: RadonSeal Deep-Penetrating Concrete Sealer

blocks.p: RadonSeal takes a different route from the repellents above. It is a water-based silicate-type sealer that reacts with lime and calcium compounds inside concrete to form a gel that fills capillaries, reducing water and vapor movement without leaving anything on the surface. That reaction needs enough reactive material in the pores, so it tends to work best on dense poured concrete and somewhat less predictably on lean, hollow block. Where it fits is a basement with block walls and a poured slab, or any wall where you want no film at all. It must go on bare, unsealed concrete, and RadonSeal publishes instructions for checking absorption before you start. Despite the name, it is not a radon mitigation system by itself; the EPA treats sealing as a supplement to active mitigation.
**Pros:** Reacts inside the concrete; nothing to peel or blister; one product for walls and slabs; clear absorption-test instructions.
**Cons:** Results on block vary more than on poured concrete; needs unsealed, unpainted surfaces; hard to judge progress.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=RadonSeal+Deep-Penetrating+Concrete+Sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Low-Odor: Seal-Once Nano+Poly Concrete and Masonry Sealer

blocks.p: Seal-Once Nano+Poly is for people who want a penetrating masonry sealer they can use in a basement, garage or workshop without solvent fumes. The maker describes it as water based, combining nano-scale particles that penetrate the masonry with a polymer that adds a light protective layer near the surface. The label lists low VOCs and soap-and-water cleanup, which makes it easy to use near living areas. On block it reduces water absorption and helps with dusting and staining, and it is also labeled for brick, concrete and stucco. It is lighter duty than a dedicated silane-siloxane on exposed exterior walls, and like other repellents it is not meant to hold back water from wet soil. Very porous or split-face block can drink more than the headline coverage suggests. Owners generally rate it well on ease of use and smell.
**Pros:** Water-based, low-VOC; penetrates and adds light surface protection; soap-and-water cleanup; works on block, brick, concrete and stucco.
**Cons:** Lighter duty than silane-siloxane products; not for water under pressure; coverage on porous block can be low.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Seal-Once+Nano+Poly+Concrete+Masonry+Sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Mixed Masonry: MasonryDefender Penetrating Water Repellent

blocks.p: MasonryDefender is a water-based silane-siloxane repellent sold for brick, block, stone and concrete. Its appeal is versatility. A house that combines a block foundation with brick veneer, a stone chimney or a stucco section can often treat several surfaces with one product. It soaks in and lines the pores rather than forming a film, so the masonry looks the same and keeps releasing vapor. Being water based, it smells less than solvent alternatives and cleans up with water while wet. It performs best on above-grade masonry exposed to rain, where it cuts absorption, efflorescence and freeze-thaw wear. It is not designed for interior basement walls that seep under pressure, and the treated surface may not accept paint later. It is mostly sold online; check the label's block-specific coverage before ordering, since porous block absorbs far more than brick.
**Pros:** Water-based silane-siloxane; invisible, breathable treatment; suits brick, block, stone and concrete; low odor.
**Cons:** Not for below-grade walls facing pressure; mostly sold online; can interfere with later painting.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=MasonryDefender+Penetrating+Water+Repellent&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Flexible Coating: Ames Block and Wall

blocks.p: Ames Block and Wall is a water-based elastomeric coating aimed at concrete block. Its strength is flexibility. Block walls develop hairline cracks along mortar joints as they settle and move with temperature, and a rigid coating can crack right along with them. An elastomeric film built to the recommended thickness stretches over that movement and keeps the wall sealed. That suits exterior block, garage walls and retaining wall faces where you want a coating instead of an invisible repellent, and interior walls damp from condensation or light wicking. It is less suited to basement walls with water pushing through from the soil, where a flexible film can lift; a cement-based waterproofer is safer there. Ames calls for multiple coats to build thickness, so coverage per gallon is lower than a thin paint. It can be painted once cured.
**Pros:** Flexible film bridges hairline cracks and joint movement; water-based cleanup; made for masonry and block; paintable after cure.
**Cons:** Thick film lowers coverage per gallon; can blister on pressurized interior walls; needs several coats.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Ames+Block+and+Wall+Liquid+Rubber&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.h: Why Do Cinder Block Walls Need a Different Sealer?

blocks.p: Because a block wall is mostly air and mortar. Sealers that work on a dense poured wall can underperform on block unless they are made or labeled for it.

A standard 8-by-8-by-16-inch block has two or three hollow cores, face shells only about an inch thick, and a lean, open-textured mix. Water that gets through the face shell drops into a core, runs down inside the wall and appears somewhere else, often at the bottom course where the wall meets the floor.

A block wall has a joint every 8 inches vertically and every 16 inches horizontally, and mortar is often more porous than the block. Hairline gaps between mortar and block are common, especially in older or settled walls. A sealer has to treat the joints as well as the faces.

Block shows efflorescence more readily and wicks water farther up the wall than poured concrete. There is less material for a reactive sealer to work with and more open pore space to fill, which is why block-specific products often call for higher solids or flood coats.

blocks.h3: Not all block is the same

blocks.p: Smooth standard block, split-face decorative block and lightweight block made with expanded aggregate all absorb differently. Rougher and lighter block drinks more product, and labels usually list a much lower coverage rate for block than their headline figure for smooth concrete.

sections.h: Penetrating Repellent or Waterproof Coating: Which Does Your Block Need?

blocks.p: Above grade, choose a penetrating repellent. Below grade on the inside of a basement, choose a waterproof coating.

Silane and siloxane repellents line the pores with a water-shedding compound and leave no visible film. They are excellent at stopping rain and splash from soaking in. For the chemistry behind them, see [silane vs siloxane](/silane-vs-siloxane-sealers/).

Cement-and-latex masonry waterproofers such as DRYLOK fill the pores and form a film on and in the surface. Their makers rate them to resist a stated hydrostatic pressure. They change the look of the wall and need a clean, bare surface to bond.

blocks.h3: Run a splash test before buying

blocks.p: Splash water on the wall. If it darkens and soaks in, the block will accept a penetrating sealer. If it beads, something is already on the surface and has to come off first, whichever product you choose.

sections.h: What Is the Best Waterproofing for a Cinder Block Basement or Foundation?

blocks.p: For interior basement block that seeps or stays damp after rain, DRYLOK Extreme brushed into bare block is the best sealer-level fix. For the outside of a foundation above grade, a silane-siloxane repellent such as Siloxa-Tek 8500 is best.

No interior sealer outlasts a gutter dumping water against the foundation. Extend downspouts, regrade soil so it slopes away from the house, and clear window wells. Our guide on [how to waterproof a basement](/how-to-waterproof-a-basement/) covers the full order of repairs, and [how to fix a damp basement](/how-to-fix-a-damp-basement/) helps you sort condensation from seepage.

Once drainage is handled, brush two coats of a pressure-rated masonry waterproofer into the bare block. For walls that are merely damp and that you want to leave unpainted, a penetrating repellent or a silicate such as RadonSeal is an option. Keep humidity down afterward; a [basement dehumidifier](/best-dehumidifier-for-basement/) helps the wall dry between storms.

Crumbling face shells, bowing walls and stair-step cracks are structural problems. Sealer will not hold failing block together. Have the wall assessed, repoint and patch what is sound, and look at drainage and full systems in our [basement waterproofing systems](/best-basement-waterproofing-systems/) guide.

Water reaches these from both sides. The back should ideally be waterproofed and drained with gravel and a pipe when built. On an existing wall, a repellent on the exposed face helps, but efflorescence continues if the soil behind stays wet.
Constant submersion needs a dedicated immersion-rated cementitious or elastomeric system, sometimes with a liner. Standard repellents are not made for it.

sections.h: What Is the Best Exterior Cement Block Sealer and Paint?

blocks.p: If you want the block to stay natural, use a penetrating repellent such as Siloxa-Tek 8500 and skip paint. If you want color, use a block filler and an acrylic masonry topcoat, or a tinted waterproofer, and skip the repellent.

Many silane-siloxane repellents leave the surface water-repellent enough that paint will not stick. If there is any chance you will want to paint later, check the data sheet for paint compatibility first. Some repellents allow painting after a cure period; many do not.

Masonry waterproofers are designed to be the finish or to take a latex topcoat after cure, and they come in tints. On an interior wall that needs moisture control and a decent look, one tinted waterproofer does both. Elastomeric coatings such as Ames Block and Wall can also be painted once cured.

If color, smoother texture and easy cleaning are the goal, use a block filler primer to close the pores, then an acrylic masonry topcoat. Our [best paint for cinder block](/best-paint-for-cinder-block/) guide covers fillers and topcoats, and the [basement floor paint](/best-basement-floor-paint/) picks cover the slab.
A penetrating repellent cannot reach the block through paint. Most of it sits on the surface and leaves a slick, blotchy finish.

sections.h: How Do You Prep Cinder Block Before Sealing?

blocks.p: Repair the mortar, remove efflorescence, strip old coatings and let the wall dry. Prep decides the result more than the product does.

Rake out loose or crumbling joints and repoint them with fresh mortar or a masonry patch, then let it cure for the time on the bag. New mortar is very alkaline, and some coatings ask for a waiting period of several weeks before sealing. Fill open holes in the block faces with patching compound.

Dry-brush the white deposits with a stiff brush, then clean with a masonry cleaner or a mild acid product made for efflorescence, following its dilution and safety directions. Rinse well. If the deposits return within weeks, water is still moving through the wall, and drainage needs attention before sealing.

A penetrating sealer cannot pass through a film, and most masonry waterproofers need bare masonry to perform as rated. Strip paint by grinding, chemical stripping or abrasive cleaning. Outdoors, a pressure washer at moderate pressure helps clean block; keep the tip back so you do not erode the mortar.

Many penetrating sealers want a surface-dry wall, often 24 to 48 hours after washing or rain, though some water-based products tolerate damp masonry; read the label. Air and surface temperatures usually need to be above 40 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, with no rain or frost expected for at least a day.

sections.h: How Do You Apply Cinder Block Sealer?

blocks.p: Spray penetrating repellents from the bottom up until they run; brush waterproof coatings hard into the block.

Use a low-pressure garden pump sprayer with a fan or cone tip. Spray from the bottom of the wall upward so the run-down saturates the area below without streaking. Many makers call for a flood coat that runs 6 to 8 inches below the spray line. On porous block, a second coat applied wet-on-wet is often recommended; follow the label timing. Back-roll with a thick-nap roller or brush to push sealer into the joints, and cover windows and plants.

Stir thoroughly. Brush the first coat hard into the block with a stiff nylon brush, working it into every pinhole and joint. Apply the second coat after the label dry time. Rolling the first coat almost always leaves pinholes, and pinholes are where water gets through.

Penetrating repellents usually look dry within hours, but each label sets its own rain-free window, and full repellency can take longer to develop than the surface takes to dry. Coatings need the recoat time on the can between coats and longer before the wall faces water. Check your product's numbers before you start an exterior job.

Ventilate well indoors, especially with solvent products, and keep ignition sources away from their vapors. Wear eye protection, gloves and a respirator suited to the product. Clean water-based products from tools while wet; solvent products need the cleanup solvent named on the label.

sections.h: How Much Sealer Does a Block Wall Need, and How Long Does It Last?

blocks.p: Plan on roughly 75 to 200 square feet per gallon per coat for penetrating repellents on standard block, and expect them to last about 5 to 10 years.

Multiply wall length by height and subtract large openings. Use the block-specific coverage from the label, not the headline figure for smooth concrete. Split-face and lightweight block can absorb far more.

Masonry waterproofers also cover less on block than on smooth concrete. DRYLOK lists roughly 75 to 100 square feet per gallon for the first coat on smooth masonry, and rough block takes more. For two coats on 500 square feet of block, plan on about 10 to 12 gallons.

Treat a few square feet, note how much it drinks and let it cure. Splash water on it. If it beads and the block stays light, your rate works. If it darkens, apply more or add a coat. The patch also shows whether the product darkens your particular block.

Makers commonly quote 5 to 10 years for silane-siloxane repellents in typical exposure, with sunny, wet walls wearing faster. Masonry waterproofers on interior walls typically last 5 to 10 years before touch-ups. Splash the wall every year or two: when water darkens the block instead of beading, reapply. Blistering, flaking or returning efflorescence on a coated wall means water is getting behind it, which points back to drainage.
Record the product and date. Sealers from different families do not always bond over each other, and knowing a wall had a repellent four years ago saves you from buying a coating that will not stick.

mistakes: A roller bridges the open pores of block and leaves pinholes that water passes straight through. Scrub the first coat of any masonry waterproofer in with a stiff nylon brush. Rollers are fine for back-rolling a penetrating sealer or for a second coat on smoother block.

White mineral deposits block penetrating sealers from the pores and push coatings off the wall as new salts form underneath. Dry-brush, clean with an efflorescence remover, rinse and dry the wall first. If the deposits return within weeks, fix the water source before sealing again.
Using a repellent against water pressure

Silane-siloxane repellents keep rain from soaking in, but they are not built to stop water pushed through a basement wall from saturated soil. For seeping interior block, use a masonry waterproofer with a labeled pressure rating, and fix gutters and grading first.

Joints are often more porous than the block and are where many leaks start. Repoint loose or cracked mortar before sealing, and work sealer into the joints with a brush or back-roller. Spraying only the block faces leaves the weakest part of the wall untreated.

Block absorbs far more than poured concrete, and labels often list lower coverage for it. Spreading a gallon to the smooth-concrete figure leaves too little in the pores to work. Test a patch, use the block coverage rate and add a second coat where the label calls for one.
bottomLine: For exterior and above-grade block, a penetrating silane-siloxane repellent such as Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500, or the lower-cost Foundation Armor SX5000, keeps the wall looking natural while stopping rain from soaking in. For interior basement block that seeps, DRYLOK Extreme brushed into bare block is the right tool, because it is built to resist water pressure from behind. Whichever you choose, fix drainage first, repoint the joints, remove efflorescence and old coatings, use the block coverage rate, and splash-test the wall every year or two.

faqs.q: What is the best sealer for cinder block walls?
faqs.a: For exterior and above-grade block, Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 is the best sealer: a silane-siloxane repellent that keeps rain out without changing the look. For interior basement block that seeps, DRYLOK Extreme is better, because its maker rates it to resist 15 psi of water pressure when brushed into bare block in two coats.

faqs.q: What is the best waterproofing for cinder block?
faqs.a: The best waterproofing for cinder block depends on where water comes from. For rain on an exterior wall, a penetrating silane-siloxane repellent works best. For water pushing through a basement wall from wet soil, use a pressure-rated masonry waterproofer such as DRYLOK Extreme, and fix gutters, downspouts and grading first.

faqs.q: How do you seal a cinder block wall?
faqs.a: Clean the wall, remove efflorescence and old coatings, repoint damaged mortar and let it dry. For exterior walls, spray a silane-siloxane repellent from the bottom up until it runs, often in two wet-on-wet coats. For seeping basement walls, brush two coats of a masonry waterproofer hard into the bare block instead.

faqs.q: Can I seal a painted block wall?
faqs.a: Not with a penetrating sealer, because it needs bare masonry to soak into and cannot pass through paint. Most masonry waterproofers also need bare surfaces to perform as rated. Strip the paint by grinding, chemical stripping or abrasive cleaning first, or, if the paint is sound and the wall is dry, repaint with a masonry paint system.

faqs.q: How often does cinder block need resealing?
faqs.a: Penetrating repellents commonly last 5 to 10 years, depending on product, sun and weather, and interior masonry waterproofers usually last 5 to 10 years before touch-ups. Splash water on the wall every year or two. If it darkens and soaks in rather than beading, the treatment has worn through and it is time to reapply.

faqs.q: Is DRYLOK a good cinder block sealer?
faqs.a: Yes, for interior basement block that seeps or stays damp. DRYLOK Extreme is a masonry waterproofer rated by its maker for 15 psi of hydrostatic pressure and designed to be brushed into block pores. For exterior above-grade block where you want a natural look and full breathability, a silane-siloxane repellent is usually the better choice.

faqs.q: Can you seal cinder block in cold weather?
faqs.a: Only within the label's limits, which are often a minimum of about 40 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit for air and surface during application and for a period afterward. Cold slows curing and can make water-based products fail. Avoid sealing when overnight frost is forecast, and wait for a mild, dry stretch for exterior walls.
